content.title: About
content.content: The dish consists of lean beef, boiled or roasted potatoes, and a mix of vegetables, excluding carrots, broccoli, and dark‑green leafy greens. It contains no sauce, making it suitable for those who prefer simple, low‑fat meals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Beef is an excellent source of complete protein, providing all essential amino acids.
Potatoes are one of the world’s most consumed tubers, rich in starch and vitamin C.
Vegetables such as zucchini, bell pepper, and tomatoes add color and flavor variety.
The absence of sauce lets the natural taste of each ingredient shine through.
The dish can be easily adapted to dietary restrictions by swapping out any of the allowed vegetables.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Beef supplies high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Beef provides vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Potassium and magnesium
items.content: Potatoes and vegetables are good sources of potassium and magnesium, which help maintain normal blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Tomatoes and bell peppers are rich in lycopene and vitamin C, antioxidants that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Low sugar content
items.content: Without sauce and with limited sweet vegetables, the dish is suitable for blood‑glucose control.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Beef, especially fattier cuts, can contain saturated fats; choosing lean cuts is recommended.

items.title: Beef allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience an allergic reaction to beef.

items.title: Potential pathogens
items.content: Undercooked meat may harbor bacteria such as Salmonella or E. coli; ensure thorough cooking.

items.title: Sodium considerations
items.content: If salt is added during preparation, monitor intake, particularly for individuals with hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, slicing the beef thinly, cutting potatoes into wedges or cubes, and cutting vegetables into bite‑size pieces. It pairs well with whole‑grain sides or a sauce‑free salad.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size bags for up to 2 months. Thaw in the fridge and reheat to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C.

content.title: About
content.content: Soy liquid coffee creamer is a plant‑based milk alternative made from soy protein, water and vegetable oils. It gives coffee a creamy texture and a mild nutty flavor, contains no lactose and is suitable for vegans.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Soy creamer is widely used in cafés and restaurants as a dairy‑free alternative.
The added vegetable oils allow the product to stay shelf‑stable before opening.
Soy protein is a complete protein, containing all essential amino acids.
Unlike nut‑based creamers, soy has a neutral taste that blends well with most coffee profiles.
In the United States soy creamer is recognized as safe by the FDA.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: One serving provides about 3–4 g of protein, helping to support muscle maintenance.

items.title: Low in sugar
items.content: Unsweetened versions are suitable for people monitoring blood glucose.

items.title: Source of vitamin B12 (fortified)
items.content: Some brands add vitamin B12, an essential nutrient for vegans.

items.title: Lactose‑free
items.content: Ideal for individuals with lactose intolerance.

items.title: Contains healthy fats
items.content: Vegetable oils provide mono‑ and poly‑unsaturated fatty acids beneficial for heart health.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: People allergic to soy may experience reactions ranging from mild to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Additive content
items.content: Some formulations contain emulsifiers and stabilizers that can cause discomfort in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Genetically modified organisms (GMOs)
items.content: Soybeans are often GMO; choose products labeled “non‑GMO” if this matters to you.

items.title: High sodium levels
items.content: Certain creamers are salted for flavor; those with hypertension should check the sodium content.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Add 1–2 tablespoons of creamer to hot coffee, latte or cappuccino. It can also be used in cold drinks, smoothies, oatmeal and baking as a milk substitute.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the unopened container in a cool, dry place away from direct light. After opening, keep refrigerated and use within 7–10 days. Discard if the product develops an off‑smell or taste.

pasta-with-tomato-based-sauce-and-poultr.title: Pasta with Tomato-Based Sauce and Poultry

content.title: About
content.content: Pasta with tomato-based sauce and poultry is a dish of cooked pasta tossed in a tomato sauce and mixed with pieces of chicken or turkey. The sauce provides a bright sweet‑tart flavor, while the poultry adds tender protein.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tomato sauce is typically made from ripe tomatoes, olive oil, garlic, and basil.
The poultry is usually grilled or sautéed to keep it juicy and flavorful.
The combination of pasta and tomato sauce is a classic Italian pairing known as "pasta al pomodoro".
The dish can be adapted to many pasta shapes: spaghetti, penne, fettuccine, etc.
Cooking tomatoes increases the bioavailability of lycopene, a powerful antioxidant.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Poultry provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Lycopene and antioxidants
items.content: Tomatoes contain lycopene, which helps protect cells from oxidative damage.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Both tomatoes and poultry supply B6 and B12 vitamins, supporting nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: When prepared with olive oil, the sauce is rich in monounsaturated fats that are heart‑friendly.

items.title: Fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain pasta adds dietary fiber, aiding digestion.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to chicken or turkey.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared sauce can be high in salt; monitor added sodium.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Traditional pasta contains gluten, making it unsuitable for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The dish can become calorie‑rich if a lot of oil or cheese is used; portion control is advised.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pasta hot, tossed with the sauce and poultry pieces. Top with grated Parmesan, fresh basil, or a drizzle of olive oil as desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Reheat with a splash of water or broth to keep the sauce from drying out.

content.title: About
content.content: Cheese pizza is a popular fast‑food item consisting of a medium‑thick crust topped with tomato sauce and a generous layer of melted cheese. It is commonly served in quick‑service restaurants and pizzerias, baked until the cheese turns golden and bubbly.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cheese pizza is one of the best‑selling items in fast‑food chains worldwide.
Traditional cheese for pizza is mozzarella, but many places blend several cheeses for a richer flavor.
A medium crust (about 0.5–0.7 cm thick) provides a balance between a crisp edge and a soft interior.
In some countries the pizza is finished with extra herbs such as oregano or basil.
Cheese pizza often serves as a base for additional toppings like pepperoni, ham, or vegetables.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: The cheese topping is rich in calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Protein rich
items.content: Both the cheese and the dough provide a good amount of animal and plant protein for tissue repair.

items.title: Contains vitamin D
items.content: Certain cheeses contain vitamin D, which aids calcium absorption.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: Cheese pizza quickly replenishes energy thanks to the combination of carbohydrates in the crust and fats in the cheese.

items.title: Probiotic potential
items.content: Some cheese varieties contain live cultures that support a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Cheese pizza is calorie‑dense, so it should be eaten in moderation, especially for weight management.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Cheese contains saturated fats, which can raise cholesterol levels if consumed excessively.

items.title: Lactose
items.content: People with lactose intolerance may experience discomfort after eating cheese pizza.

items.title: Salt
items.content: Both cheese and sauce often contain significant sodium, which can be a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Some individuals may have an allergic reaction to casein, the main protein in cheese.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cheese pizza is typically enjoyed hot, sliced into wedges. You can add fresh herbs, a drizzle of olive oil, or a spicy sauce to taste. It is often served with a side salad of fresh vegetables.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftover pizza in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Reheat in an oven or grill to restore a crisp crust.

pork-chow-mein-or-chop-suey-no-noodles.title: Pork Chow Mein or Chop Suey, No Noodles

content.title: About
content.content: Pork Chow Mein without noodles (also known as Chop Suey) is a classic Chinese‑style stir‑fry that features tender strips of pork, crisp vegetables, soy sauce and aromatic spices, but omits the noodles. The result is a flavorful, protein‑rich dish suitable for low‑carb diets.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditional chow mein is usually served with egg noodles, yet many Chinese households prepare a noodle‑free version for health reasons.
Chop suey originated in the United States as an adaptation of Chinese cuisine by immigrant cooks.
Pork is often marinated in a mixture of soy sauce, rice wine and ginger to enhance its flavor.
Typical vegetables include bell pepper, carrot, bamboo shoots and shiitake mushrooms.
The dish is cooked quickly over high heat in a wok, preserving the crunch of the vegetables.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Pork provides complete protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Thiamine, niacin and vitamin B6 in pork support energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Pork supplies iron, zinc and selenium, important for immune function and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Without noodles the dish fits well into keto and other low‑carb eating plans.

items.title: Fiber from vegetables
items.content: Bell pepper, carrot and bamboo shoots add dietary fiber that aids digestion.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Soy sauce can add a lot of salt; choose reduced‑sodium versions if needed.

items.title: Allergy concerns
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to soy sauce, sesame oil or certain vegetables.

items.title: Meat quality
items.content: Select fresh, lean cuts of pork to reduce the risk of food‑borne illness.

items.title: Proper cooking
items.content: Pork should reach an internal temperature of at least 63 °C (145 °F) to ensure safety.

content.title: How to Cook
content.content: Slice pork into thin strips and marinate in soy sauce, ginger and garlic for 15‑20 minutes. Heat a wok with a small amount of oil, stir‑fry the pork until browned, then add sliced bell pepper, carrot, bamboo shoots and mushrooms. Cook on high heat for 5‑7 minutes, stirring constantly. Adjust seasoning with a splash of broth or additional soy sauce if needed. Serve hot.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze up to 1 month after cooling, using a freezer‑safe bag.

rice-white-with-dark-green-vegetables-an.title: White Rice with Dark Green Vegetables and Tomatoes

content.title: About
content.content: This dish consists of boiled white rice, dark green vegetables (such as broccoli, spinach or green beans) and tomatoes or a tomato‑based sauce, prepared without added fat. The combination provides a balanced mix of carbohydrates, fiber, vitamins and minerals while keeping the calorie count low.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: White rice is a source of quickly digestible carbohydrates, making it a good energy boost after exercise.
Dark green vegetables are rich in chlorophyll, which supports the body’s detoxification processes.
Tomatoes contain lycopene – a powerful antioxidant that becomes more bioavailable after cooking.
A fat‑free preparation fits well into calorie‑restricted and low‑fat diets.
The rice‑vegetable blend supplies all essential amino acids.

items.title: Energy support
items.content: White rice rapidly supplies glucose, helping maintain energy levels during activity.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Rice provides thiamine, niacin and vitamin B6, which are involved in carbohydrate metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Tomatoes and dark green vegetables deliver vitamin C, vitamin K and lycopene, protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Digestive health
items.content: Fiber from the vegetables promotes intestinal motility and supports a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: The absence of added fats makes the dish suitable for heart‑healthy eating plans.

items.title: Glycemic index
items.content: White rice has a high glycemic index, so people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Tomato allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to tomatoes or tomato sauce.

items.title: Lack of dietary fat
items.content: Without added fat, the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) may be reduced; include healthy fats in other meals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish as a side with meat, fish or legumes. It reheats well in the microwave or on the stovetop, and fresh herbs can be added for extra flavor. Vary the dark green vegetables for different textures and tastes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. When reheating, ensure it reaches an internal temperature of 75 °C.

content.title: About
content.content: Salami is a smoked‑cured sausage made from any type of meat (beef, pork, poultry, etc.). The process involves salting, seasoning with spices, and long aging, which gives it its characteristic aroma and firm texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Salami originated in Italy in the 19th century and quickly spread worldwide.
Traditionally a blend of beef and pork is used, but modern versions may contain turkey, chicken, or even venison.
Dry aging can last from a few weeks to several months, depending on the desired flavor intensity.
Salami is often served thinly sliced as a snack, in sandwiches, or paired with cheese and wine.
Reduced sodium (996 mg per 100 g) makes it more suitable for those monitoring salt intake.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Salami provides high‑quality animal protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: The meat in salami supplies heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Salami contains B12, B6, and niacin, supporting nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Reduced sodium
items.content: Lower salt content (996 mg/100 g) helps with blood pressure control.

items.title: Zinc content
items.content: Zinc in salami contributes to immune function and wound healing.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Salami contains saturated fats, so it should be eaten in moderation, especially by those with cardiovascular concerns.

items.title: Nitrite additives
items.content: Nitrites are often used to preserve color and prevent bacterial growth; excessive intake may be harmful.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may have allergic reactions to specific meats used in salami.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Despite reduction, 996 mg of sodium is still notable; people with hypertension should account for total daily salt intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice salami thinly and enjoy as a snack, add to sandwiches, salads, pasta, or pizza. It also works well in cooked dishes where it releases flavor during baking.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store salami in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C in its original packaging or an airtight container. For longer storage (over 2‑3 weeks) freeze it to preserve flavor and prevent spoilage.

taco-or-tostada-salad-with-meat.title: Taco or Tostada Salad with Meat

content.title: About
content.content: Taco or tostada salad with meat is a Mexican‑style dish that combines crunchy tostada shells or soft taco tortillas, fresh vegetables, aromatic spices, and sautéed meat (commonly beef, chicken or pork). It is usually served with salsa, guacamole or sour cream.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: A tostada is a fried corn tortilla that becomes crisp, a staple in central Mexico.
Traditional tacos use soft corn or flour tortillas that are folded and eaten by hand.
The meat is often marinated in lime juice, chili, cumin and coriander for a bright flavor.
The salad typically includes tomatoes, corn, beans, avocado and lime, balancing sour, sweet and spicy notes.
Tacos became widely popular in the United States in the 1960s thanks to the Taco Bell chain, leading to countless variations.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: The meat provides complete, high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Beef and chicken supply B12, niacin and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Fiber from vegetables
items.content: Fresh veggies and beans add dietary fiber that promotes healthy digestion.

items.title: Healthy fats from avocado
items.content: Avocado contributes monounsaturated fats that are heart‑friendly.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Tomatoes, corn and spices (chili, coriander) are rich in antioxidants that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Prepared sauces and seasonings can be salty; people with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Corn or wheat allergy
items.content: Corn‑based tostadas may trigger reactions in corn‑allergic individuals, while flour tortillas can affect those with gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Spicy ingredients
items.content: Chili peppers may irritate the stomach of people with gastritis or ulcers.

items.title: Calorie density
items.content: Meat, avocado and sauces make the dish relatively calorie‑rich; moderation is advised for weight‑control diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the salad on top of tostada shells or inside soft taco tortillas, then add guacamole, salsa, sour cream and a sprinkle of grated cheese. It can also be tossed together in a bowl and eaten as a regular salad.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Prepared salad keeps in the refrigerator in an airtight container for up to 2 days. Store tostadas separately in a dry place to stay crisp. Re‑heat tostadas quickly in a skillet before serving.
